name: Heightpill / height blackpill

lead: The heightpill is the belief, common on looksmaxxing forums, that a man's height is one of the biggest factors in dating and social outcomes. For readers it works as a motivator: it points attention to looking taller through lifts, posture, tailoring and other height-adding choices.

Studies report that many women prefer taller male partners on average and that shorter men are rated less favourably. Other work finds people trade height against traits like income and education, and that preferences vary across cultures.

paras: It is a framework rather than a product. People who adopt it usually respond by working on the height they can influence: shoe lifts, posture, clothes cut to lengthen the frame, haircuts, and photo framing. Some look into more drastic height-altering measures covered in other entries.
The main documented concern is psychological distress among teens and men who fixate on height. The measures people reach for to change height carry their own medical risks, covered in those entries.

angle.text: Looksmaxxing forums use the heightpill to describe the belief that height strongly shapes a man's dating outcomes, which drives interest in lifts, styling and, for some, surgery. Research shows many women prefer taller partners on average, with the preference varying by culture and trading off against other traits.

lead: The heightpill (or height blackpill) is a belief, widespread on looksmaxxing forums, that a man's height is among the most influential factors in dating and social outcomes. It sits inside the "pill" vocabulary of online manosphere communities, where a "pill" names a supposedly uncomfortable truth, and the black pill more broadly holds that fixed physical traits shape dating outcomes.[1]

For people who hold it, the heightpill is the reason height gets so much attention in looksmaxxing: it motivates interest in lifts and footwear, posture, adolescent growth optimisation, and limb-lengthening surgery as ways to look taller. Adherents commonly describe a threshold, often framed in feet and inches, below which they say a man is at a major disadvantage.[2][3]

Published research on height and attraction shows that many women prefer taller male partners and that shorter men are rated less favourably on average, while other work finds that people trade height off against income, education and other traits, and that preferences vary across cultures.[4][5]
infobox: Height preferences studied; strong claims about decisive effect are disputed

paras: The heightpill holds that height functions as a gatekeeping trait. Forum posts describe being below a given height as a lasting social handicap, and some state that average height is no longer "enough".[2] One looksmax.org poster argues that men of 6 feet and above "have presence" entering a room, and that shorter men are treated differently regardless of face.[3]

Related terms include "manlet" for a short man, and discussions often rank height alongside face, frame and race as fixed traits. Some posters argue that masculine traits such as height, frame, voice and large hands can outweigh a good-looking face.[2][6]

Wikipedia's incel article traces the "pill" language to the red pill in The Matrix, with the black pill a more fatalistic variant holding that genetics largely determine dating success. It notes that people in these communities attribute their lower social status partly to physical stature and appearance, while some still pursue improvement through looksmaxxing.[1]

Sociological and economic literature on height discrimination ("heightism", coined in 1971) reports that taller men were more likely to marry and have more children in several historical datasets, and that American women in one widely cited study preferred taller partners, with shorter men needing higher incomes to be rated equally appealing. In the same literature, average-height and tall men were rated similarly, with shorter men viewed less favourably.[4]

The same source reports that people trade height off against other qualities: an Indonesian study found men compensated for shorter stature with higher wages and women with more education, a Hungarian survey found most respondents favoured average to moderately tall heights, and a study of the Hadza foragers found height did not factor into mate choice, which the article takes to indicate that the preference is shaped by culture.[4]

Beyond dating, studies cited in reference works report that height correlates positively with income and occupational success in many settings, though part of the gap may be explained by sex or socioeconomic status.[4][5]

Communities that hold the heightpill discuss responses such as limb-lengthening surgery, growth hormone in adolescence, and footwear, as well as posture and "height-maxxing" techniques. Forum posts note that some teenagers consider growth hormone ineffective once their expected final height is set.[2] Medical sources on these methods are covered in their own entries.
No studies found testing the heightpill as a theory. Observational and survey studies of height and partner preference, summarised above, exist in the wider literature on height discrimination.[4]

lore.intro: On looksmaxxing forums the heightpill is treated as one of the main "pills", and threads on it recur frequently.[2][3]

claims.claim: Height is the single most decisive trait for a man's dating success.
Looks or other traits cannot compensate for being short.
Masculine traits such as height, frame, voice and large hands can outweigh facial looks.
The importance of height is universal and biological.

timeline.event: Sociologist Saul Feldman coins the term "heightism" for height-based discrimination.[4]
